title: What Is Claude Code
summary: An agentic CLI that reads your repo, edits files, runs tests, and commits — all with permission gates you control.

content_items.text: Claude Code is not autocomplete. It is an agent that operates a real terminal: it reads files, runs commands, writes code, and waits for your approval at each risky step. It lives in your terminal first, but the same agent now runs in the VS Code and JetBrains extensions, a desktop app, and on the web at claude.ai/code — everything in this course transfers.

The mental shift: instead of typing characters, you describe outcomes. Instead of clicking Run, you watch the agent run things and read back the output. Instead of debugging line by line, you tell it what's broken and it iterates until tests pass.

Vibe coding is the practice of working at this altitude. You stay in flow on the what, the agent handles the how. The skills you'll build in this course are the prompts, patterns, and guardrails that make this loop reliable.

A CLI agent that reads your repo, runs commands, and edits files with your permission.

A code review bot that comments on GitHub PRs.

options.text: Letting the AI ship code with no oversight.

Operating at the level of outcomes; the agent handles the how.

terms.definition: A model wired to tools and a loop: it reads, acts, checks the result, and goes again until the task is done or you stop it.
Building software by describing what you want to an agent and judging the result rather than reading every line of code.

title: Your First Conversation
summary: Watch the agentic loop in action: a single prompt, a tool call, a result, an answer. This is the heartbeat.

content_items.text: Every Claude Code interaction is a loop. You speak. The agent decides if it needs information from your machine. If yes, it calls a tool — Read, Bash, Grep — and waits for the result. Then it speaks again, and the loop continues until the task is done.
Below is a sandbox replay of a real first conversation. Watch how the agent uses Read to actually look at the file before answering — this is what separates an agent from autocomplete.

It always reads README.md before doing anything else.

options.text: User → Read → Done.

title: The Agentic Loop
summary: Plan → act → observe → adjust. Understanding this loop is the difference between fighting the agent and flowing with it.

content_items.text: Every step the agent takes follows the same four-beat rhythm. Plan: decide what to do next based on the current goal and context. Act: call a tool — read a file, run a command, edit code. Observe: read the tool's output. Adjust: update the plan based on what came back, then loop.

When you understand this rhythm, two things happen. First, you stop interrupting mid-loop — you let the agent finish its observation before adding new constraints. Second, you start writing prompts that front-load the constraints, because constraints added before a loop starts are cheap; constraints added in the middle force a re-plan.

Concretely: 'Refactor the auth module. Keep the public API stable. Add tests for every changed file.' is a complete loop input. 'Refactor the auth module' followed by 'oh and don't break the API' two minutes later is a re-plan that costs you turns.

quizzes.question: Q1. Which sequence describes one beat of the agentic loop?

Think, write, test, review.

quizzes.question: Q2. Why is front-loading constraints in your prompt cheaper than adding them later?

options.text: It uses fewer tokens overall.

Front-loaded constraints unlock a faster model.

title: CLAUDE.md and Project Memory
summary: Project-level instructions the agent loads automatically. The single highest-leverage file in your repo when you work this way.

content_items.text: Every time you launch Claude Code in a directory that has a CLAUDE.md, the file is injected into the agent's context. It's how you teach the agent your conventions, your stack, and your taste — once, durably.

Good CLAUDE.md files are short and specific: things the agent could not figure out by reading the code. Bad CLAUDE.md files restate what's obvious from package.json. The /init slash command writes a starter file you then prune. Mid-session, start any message with # to fold a new rule into memory without breaking flow.

title: Reading and Editing Files
summary: The agent navigates, edits, and verifies across multiple files in one turn.

content_items.text: Read pulls a file into context. Edit replaces an exact string. Write creates or overwrites a file. The agent picks the right tool for the size of the change — Edit for surgical work, Write for new files.

Watch the agent stay disciplined: it reads before it edits, and after every edit it can re-read to confirm the change took. This is how reliability is built into agentic workflows — not through promises, but through verifiable observations.

quizzes.question: Q1. Why did the agent re-read the file after editing?

options.text: To make the conversation longer.
To verify the edit landed correctly before claiming success.
Because Edit doesn't actually write to disk.
It's required by the Edit tool.

title: Searching the Codebase
summary: Glob finds files by pattern. Grep finds content inside them. Knowing which to use is half the speed.

content_items.text: Glob is for 'where does X live': **/*.test.ts finds every test file. Grep is for 'who uses Y': useAuth\( finds every call site. The mistake new users make is greping when they should glob — slower, noisier.
When you're not sure, ask the agent for a plan first. It will pick correctly more often than you do.

quizzes.question: Q1. When should you use Glob over Grep?

options.text: When you want to find file *names* matching a pattern, not their contents.
Always — Grep is slower.
When you're searching binary files.
When you don't know what you're looking for.

title: Running Tests with Claude
summary: Tight feedback loops: run, read failure, fix, run again — without you driving.

content_items.text: Once tests are wired up, the agent can drive the red→green loop on its own. You describe what should be true; it writes the assertion; it watches the test fail; it edits the implementation; it re-runs until green.
The skill here is trusting the loop. Don't peek at every iteration — let it run, then review the diff at the end.

quizzes.question: Q1. What's the value of letting the agent run the test *before* writing the implementation?

options.text: It's faster.
It proves the test actually fails — a passing assertion you didn't see fail is unverified.
It avoids running the test twice.
It saves on tokens.

title: Git Operations and Commits
summary: Letting the agent stage, write a real commit message, and stop short of pushing.

content_items.text: Claude Code can stage changes, write commit messages, and even create branches — but by default it will not push or force-push without explicit confirmation. Treat git operations like any other risky tool: gate them through your approval.

steps.title: Ask for a commit
steps.body: After making changes, ask the agent to commit. It will run status, diff, and log to read the project's commit style first.
steps.verify: VerifyYou see Bash calls for git status, git diff, git log, then a commit with a message that matches the repo's tone.

steps.title: Refuse the auto-push
steps.body: If the agent offers to push, say no. Push is a shared-state action — keep that on your hands.
steps.verify: VerifyThe session ends with the commit local; you can git log -1 and inspect.

steps.title: Reset gracefully
steps.body: If the message or content is wrong, ask the agent to soft-reset and try again, rather than amending.
steps.verify: Verifygit status shows the changes back in your working tree, ready to be re-committed.

title: Multi-File Refactors
summary: Renames, signature changes, and dependency updates done as one coherent change.

content_items.text: The thing humans hate most about refactors is the bookkeeping: every call site, every import, every test. The agent eats that for breakfast — as long as you give it a clear shape change up front.
Pattern: state the rename or signature change in one sentence. Let the agent do a Grep for call sites. Then ask it to update all of them in a single sweep, run the tests, and report.

quizzes.question: Q1. What gives multi-file refactors their reliability?

options.text: The agent's memory.
Grep finds every call site, then a coordinated edit + test run proves nothing was missed.
The agent reads the entire codebase into context.
Static type checking.

terms.definition: A mechanical pass/fail test the harness or CI runs on the agent's work: types, lint, tests, build. Cheap, fast, no judgement.

title: Debugging with Claude
summary: Hypothesis → instrumentation → evidence → fix. The structured-debug pattern.

content_items.text: Most debugging fails because people guess. The structured pattern is: state a hypothesis ('I think X is null because Y'), instrument to test it (add a log, write a failing test), observe, then either confirm and fix or update the hypothesis.
The agent is great at this if you ask it to follow the pattern explicitly. Without that prompt, it will sometimes leap to a fix without proving the cause.

quizzes.question: Q1. Why is writing a failing test before fixing a bug valuable?

options.text: It satisfies the test runner.
It proves the cause and prevents regression. A fix without a failing test is unverified.
It's faster than debugging by hand.
It's required by Claude Code.

title: Slash Commands
summary: The built-ins worth memorizing: /init, /clear, /resume, /compact, /rewind, /model.

content_items.text: Slash commands are first-class shortcuts in Claude Code. Each one fires a specific behavior — write a memory file, clear context, summarize the session. Knowing them is the difference between fighting the chat and steering it.

steps.title: Try /init
steps.body: Generates or updates CLAUDE.md by reading your repo. Use it once per project, then prune the output.
steps.verify: VerifyA CLAUDE.md is written or updated at the project root.

steps.title: Use /clear when context drifts
steps.body: /clear wipes the conversation but keeps your project memory. Run it when you switch tasks — fresh context produces sharper plans.
steps.verify: VerifyThe chat starts a new session; CLAUDE.md is still loaded.

steps.title: Resume a long session with /resume
steps.body: If you closed Claude Code and want to pick up where you left off, /resume loads the previous session.
steps.verify: VerifyThe agent restates the goal of the prior session before you continue.

steps.title: Compact when you must keep going
steps.body: /compact summarizes the conversation so far so context doesn't blow up. Less destructive than /clear when you need continuity.
steps.verify: VerifyThe session continues with a much smaller context window than before.

steps.title: Rewind when a change goes sideways
steps.body: Claude Code checkpoints your files before each change. /rewind (or double-tap Escape) opens the checkpoint picker — restore the code, the conversation, or both. It's the undo button that makes bold experiments cheap.
steps.verify: VerifyA picker lists recent checkpoints; selecting one restores that state without touching your git history.

steps.title: Match the model to the task
steps.body: /model switches models mid-session. Reach for the frontier tier (Opus 4.8, or the Claude 5 family where available) on hard refactors and planning; drop to Haiku 4.5 for fast, cheap iteration on simple edits.
steps.verify: VerifyThe picker shows the active model; the status line reflects your choice on the next turn.

title: Writing Your Own Slash Command
summary: A markdown file in .claude/commands/ becomes a callable workflow.

content_items.text: Custom slash commands are how you turn a repeated prompt into a one-keystroke action. Write the prompt as markdown, save it under .claude/commands/, type /your-command, done.

The use cases are endless: /review-pr, /write-tests, /draft-changelog, /find-todos. Each one is a small specialized agent run you've made repeatable. And when a command outgrows one file — it needs reference docs, scripts, or templates — graduate it to an Agent Skill (next lesson).

steps.body: Write a markdown file with the prompt you want fired. Use $ARGUMENTS for inline arguments.
steps.verify: Verify.claude/commands/review-pr.md exists with that content.

steps.title: Use it
steps.body: From any session in that repo, type the command.
steps.verify: VerifyThe agent runs the prompt with 'auth module' substituted into $ARGUMENTS.

steps.title: Iterate
steps.body: Run the command. If the output is too long, too short, or wrong — edit the markdown and re-run. Slash commands evolve like any other prompt.

title: Agent Skills
summary: Folders of expertise the agent loads on demand. Commands are prompts you fire; skills are capabilities Claude reaches for itself.

content_items.text: An Agent Skill is a folder with a SKILL.md inside: instructions, plus any scripts, templates, or reference docs the job needs. The crucial difference from slash commands: you invoke a command, but Claude invokes a skill — whenever your request matches the skill's description.

Skills use progressive disclosure. Only the name and one-line description sit in context; the full instructions load when the skill fires. That's why a project can carry dozens of skills without bloating every session — and why the description line is the part worth sweating.
The same format works across Claude Code, claude.ai, and the API, so a skill you write for your repo travels with you.

steps.title: Scaffold a skill
steps.body: Project skills live in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Personal ones live in ~/.claude/skills/ and follow you across projects.
steps.verify: VerifyThe folder exists at your project root.

steps.title: Write SKILL.md
steps.body: Frontmatter carries the name and — most importantly — the description Claude matches against. The body is the playbook.
steps.verify: VerifySKILL.md exists with frontmatter and numbered instructions.

steps.title: Trigger it naturally
steps.body: Don't type a slash command — just ask in plain language and watch Claude pick the skill up.
steps.verify: VerifyThe transcript shows the skill loading, then the playbook being followed step by step.

steps.title: Tune the description
steps.body: If the skill didn't fire, the description didn't match how you actually ask. Rewrite it with the phrases you'd really use — that line is the routing layer.
steps.verify: VerifyThe same natural-language ask now reliably triggers the skill.

title: Subagents and the Agent Tool
summary: When to delegate to a subagent vs do it inline. Context budgets explained.

content_items.text: A subagent is a fresh Claude session the main agent spawns to do a specific task. It has its own context window — so it can read 50 files without polluting your main thread. When it finishes, it returns a summary, not the raw work.

Use subagents for: open-ended research ('find every place that uses our deprecated API'), large lookups, or work where the findings matter more than the steps. Don't use them for tasks where you need the main agent to keep that context — refactors, debugging, anything stateful.

The trap: subagents are expensive. If you fire three in parallel for a task you could do inline, you've burned tokens for nothing. The rule of thumb: would I want to read all the intermediate output? If no, delegate.

You can also define named subagents — a markdown file under .claude/agents/ with its own system prompt and tool allowlist — and Claude routes matching work to them automatically. /agents lists what's available. A read-only code-reviewer is the classic first one to write.

options.text: Always — fresh context is always better.
When the task is open-ended research and you want the findings, not the intermediate steps, in the main context.
For any task longer than 5 minutes.
Never — they waste tokens.

options.text: The full transcript of its work.
A summary it composes itself; the intermediate steps are not visible to the main thread.
Nothing — they're fire and forget.

title: Plan Mode
summary: Read-only thinking before any edit. The cure for premature commitment.

content_items.text: In Plan Mode the agent can read, search, and reason — but it cannot edit, run shell commands that modify state, or commit. It produces a plan you approve before it gets the tools to act. Toggle it with Shift+Tab, or launch straight into it with claude --permission-mode plan.
When to use it: anything that touches more than two files, anything you're not 100% sure how to scope, anything where the wrong approach costs more than waiting one extra turn.

quizzes.question: Q1. Why does Plan Mode disallow edits?

options.text: Edits are slow.
It forces the agent to articulate the full approach before any state changes — so you can correct course before damage is done.
It saves tokens.
Tools don't work in plan mode.

terms.definition: A read-only agent mode: the agent may search and read, but must propose a plan for your approval before it edits anything.
One continuous run with an agent, from an empty context to the moment you clear it, close it, or hand its work off.

title: Hooks: Pre and Post Tool
summary: Run a script before or after each tool call. Lint on every edit; auto-test on commit.

content_items.text: Hooks let you wedge custom logic into the agent's loop. PreToolUse fires before the agent calls a tool — you can rewrite, allow, or block. PostToolUse fires after — perfect for running formatters, type-checks, or tests automatically. Other events cover the rest of the lifecycle (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop), but the Pre/PostToolUse pair does most of the real work.

Configured in .claude/settings.json. The biggest win: post-edit linting. Every time the agent edits a file, your linter runs; if it fails, the agent sees the failure and self-corrects. You never see the broken state.

steps.title: Open the settings file
steps.body: Create or open the project settings.
steps.verify: VerifyAn empty or existing settings.json opens.

steps.title: Add a post-edit format hook
steps.body: Run prettier on every Edit/Write to keep code consistent without asking the agent.
steps.verify: VerifyAfter the agent edits a file, you see prettier run in the tool stream.

steps.title: Add a pre-bash safety hook
steps.body: Block the agent from running risky commands without asking. The hook intercepts and you decide.
steps.verify: VerifyBash calls now route through your script. Add a deny list for things like rm -rf / and git push --force.

title: MCP Servers
summary: Pluggable tools beyond the built-ins. Connecting your database, your Slack, your Linear.

content_items.text: MCP — Model Context Protocol — is the standard Claude Code uses to talk to external tools. Need the agent to query your Postgres? Hit your Linear tickets? Read your Notion? Each capability is an MCP server you add to the agent's toolbelt.

MCP servers are processes (local or remote) that expose tools the agent can call. The protocol is open and language-agnostic — you can write your own in an afternoon, and thousands are already published. Adding one is a single command — claude mcp add — and remote servers authenticate with OAuth via /mcp.
The mental model: built-in tools give the agent a terminal. MCP servers extend that terminal to your whole stack.

quizzes.question: Q1. What does MCP do?

options.text: It encrypts messages between you and Claude.
It's the standard protocol for plugging external tools into the agent — databases, APIs, SaaS — so they appear as callable tools alongside Read and Bash.
It compresses context.
It's a slash command framework.

terms.definition: Model Context Protocol: an open standard for plugging external tool servers into any agent harness.

title: Spec → Tests → Code
summary: Front-load tests; let the agent fill them in. Why this beats spec → code → tests.

content_items.text: When the spec exists as failing tests first, the agent has a measurable target. It writes code, runs tests, sees red, edits, runs again. The loop terminates only when the spec is satisfied.
When you write code first and tests after, the tests describe what the code already does — not what it should do. They lose their value as a forcing function.

steps.title: Describe the spec in prose
steps.body: Don't dive into types yet. Write 4-6 sentences that describe the behavior, the inputs, the outputs, the edge cases.
steps.verify: VerifyThe spec is short, behavior-focused, and lists at least 2 edge cases.

steps.title: Have the agent write tests first
steps.body: Ask explicitly for tests before any implementation.
steps.verify: VerifyYou see a test file and a failing run with N failures, where N matches the assertions.

steps.title: Now write the code
steps.body: Ask for the implementation. Iterate until green.
steps.verify: VerifyTests pass. Code is shaped by the spec, not by the first thing that came to mind.

quizzes.question: Q1. Why are tests written *before* the implementation more valuable than tests written after?

options.text: They run faster.
They describe the spec, not the code; they force the implementation to satisfy a target rather than rationalize what's there.
There's no difference.
Test-after is faster but less correct.

terms.definition: A written description of what to build and how you'll know it's right, agreed before the agent starts writing code.

title: Iterative Refinement
summary: Three small turns beat one giant turn. How to size a single ask.

content_items.text: A common failure mode: 'Build the entire dashboard. Use these 8 components, fetch from these 3 endpoints, handle loading/error/empty states, add tests.' The agent does 60% well and 40% wrong, and now you have a 400-line diff to debug.

Better: ship one slice at a time. Empty state. Loading state. One endpoint. One component. Each turn ends with a runnable, testable artifact. You compound small correct steps; you don't debug a huge wrong step.

quizzes.question: Q1. Why does sizing tasks small make agentic work more reliable?

options.text: Agents have a strict turn limit.
Each small step ends in a verifiable artifact; mistakes are isolated and cheap to revert. Big steps compound errors.
Small tasks are faster.
It saves tokens.

lesson_num_title: 21. When to Interrupt vs Let It Run
title: When to Interrupt vs Let It Run
summary: Reading the loop. Knowing when re-planning is cheaper than waiting.

content_items.text: The instinct to interrupt the moment you see something off is usually wrong. Most of the time, the agent's next observation will catch the error itself. Interrupting throws away that self-correction.

The right time to interrupt: when the agent is about to do something destructive (rm, git push --force, a dangerous DB query) — that's why approval gates exist. Or when you realize the goal you stated was wrong and continuing would compound the mistake.
Bad reasons to interrupt: 'I can see this won't work' (let it find out and self-correct), 'It's slow' (wait for the result), 'I have a faster idea' (queue it for after this turn).

quizzes.question: Q1. Which is a *good* reason to interrupt mid-loop?

options.text: You think the next step is wrong.
It's taking longer than you expected.
You realize the goal you stated was wrong, and continuing under the wrong goal will compound the mistake.
You want to add a different feature.

title: Code Review with Claude
summary: Using the agent as a second pair of eyes on your own diff before you push.

content_items.text: Self-review with the agent catches the things you can't see anymore — the assumptions baked into your own diff. It's not a replacement for human review; it's the spell-check of code.
Best framing: 'Review this diff like a senior who hates churn. What are the missing tests, the leaky abstractions, the unsafe assumptions?'

quizzes.question: Q1. What's a useful framing for self-review with the agent?

options.text: Ask if the code 'looks good.'
Ask the agent to act like a senior reviewer hostile to churn, and be specific about what to flag (missing tests, unsafe input, leaky abstractions).
Tell it to rewrite the code.
Ask for a summary.

terms.definition: A person reading the agent's work before it ships. The only step that judges whether the change is right, not just whether it passes.

title: The Pair-Programming Flow
summary: How to stay in flow when the agent is your driver and you're the navigator.

content_items.text: In classical pair programming, one person types (driver) and one thinks (navigator). With the agent, you're the navigator. Your job is shape, intent, and quality — not characters.

The pattern: state intent in 2-3 sentences. Watch the agent act. Read the diff. Approve, redirect, or correct. Don't context-switch back to writing characters yourself; if something's wrong, say what's wrong and let the agent fix it.

Two skills compound here. First, learn to articulate intent precisely — vague prompts produce vague code. Second, learn to read diffs faster than you can write them. That's where the speedup actually lives.

quizzes.question: Q1. In an agent-driven pair, what's your role?

options.text: Type the code while the agent watches.
Articulate intent and review diffs; let the agent type.
Write tests only.
Approve every keystroke.

terms.definition: A model wired to tools and a loop: it reads, acts, checks the result, and goes again until the task is done or you stop it.

title: Building a Next.js Feature
summary: From issue to deployed PR. A complete loop on a realistic Next.js codebase.

content_items.text: End-to-end: an issue describes a feature; the agent reads the codebase, writes the route, the page, the test, opens a PR. Watch how a single well-scoped prompt produces a reviewable change.

quizzes.question: Q1. Why does the prompt include both the route, the data shape, and the test in one breath?

options.text: To minimize turns.
Front-loading constraints (where copy lives, what to test) makes the loop converge in one pass instead of three.
It's required.
The agent can't handle multi-step asks.

title: Writing Tests-First
summary: Red, green, refactor — but the agent does the typing.

content_items.text: The tightest TDD loop you'll ever drive. You describe the spec; the agent writes the failing test; the agent writes the implementation; you review; the agent refactors. You do almost no typing — but you steer with precision.

quizzes.question: Q1. What does seeing all 5 tests fail before any implementation prove?

options.text: Nothing — it's just a checkpoint.
That the tests are real and exercise behavior that doesn't exist yet — they couldn't have been satisfied accidentally.
That the agent is slow.
That the spec is wrong.

terms.definition: A model wired to tools and a loop: it reads, acts, checks the result, and goes again until the task is done or you stop it.

title: Migrating Legacy Code
summary: TypeScript adoption in a JS codebase, one module at a time, tests stay green.

content_items.text: Big migrations fail when teams treat them as one push. The agent-driven approach is the opposite: migrate one leaf module first, ship it, do the next leaf. The repo is always green; you can stop at any point.

quizzes.question: Q1. What's the key constraint that makes leaf-by-leaf migration safe?

options.text: It's faster.
Existing tests must stay green after every step. The repo is shippable at every commit.
TypeScript is forgiving.
Leaves don't have dependencies.

title: Shipping to Production
summary: Pre-deploy checks, the migration script, the rollback plan.

content_items.text: Production deploys are the riskiest moment in the loop. Use the agent as a checklist enforcer: it verifies tests, types, lint, migrations, env vars, and prepares the rollback before you press the button.

steps.title: Run the pre-deploy gauntlet
steps.body: Tests, types, lint, build — all four green before anything touches prod.
steps.verify: VerifyEither all four pass, or you get a precise failure to triage.

steps.title: Inspect the migration
steps.body: Have the agent read the migration that's about to run, summarize what it changes, and flag any non-reversible operations.
steps.verify: VerifyYou get a 1-paragraph summary plus an explicit list of irreversible ops (DROPs, NOT NULL on backfilled columns, etc.).

steps.title: Draft the rollback plan
steps.body: Before deploying, have the agent write the rollback steps you'll run if something breaks.
steps.verify: VerifyA markdown file exists with the rollback steps before you deploy. Future you will thank present you.

quizzes.question: Q1. Why draft the rollback plan *before* deploying instead of after a problem?

options.text: It's faster.
Under pressure your judgment is worse; pre-written rollback steps are saner than improvised ones.
Rollbacks are easier to plan after.
It's required by SOC 2.

title: Capstone: Ship a Side Project
summary: Pick a real idea, scope it, build it with Claude Code, deploy it. Course-end project.

content_items.text: The capstone is the proof. Pick a small but real product idea — something a few people would actually use. Scope it down to what you can ship in one weekend with the agent driving.
Constraints: must be something you'd be willing to put your name on, must be deployed somewhere a human can visit, must have at least one test that exercises the happy path. That's it.

steps.title: Pick the idea — small and real
steps.body: Not a clone of Twitter. Not 'a CRM for X.' Pick one tiny tool with one user — maybe yourself. A bookmark organizer. A meeting-notes summarizer. A tip calculator with split logic. The smaller, the better.
steps.verify: VerifyYour idea fits in three sentences. If it doesn't, scope down.

steps.title: Set up the repo with the agent
steps.body: Use Claude Code to scaffold. Pick a stack you mostly know — capstone is not the time to learn three new frameworks.
steps.verify: VerifyYou have a runnable app on localhost:3000.

steps.title: Build the spine in 3-4 small turns
steps.body: Use what you learned: spec → tests → code, small slices, mark-complete on each. Each turn ends in a runnable, testable state.
steps.verify: VerifyEach turn produces a slice you could ship. If a turn produces something not-shippable, scope it smaller next time.

steps.title: Deploy
steps.body: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, Railway — pick whichever has a one-command deploy.
steps.verify: VerifyThere is a public URL. You can text it to a friend.

steps.title: Write a 1-paragraph postmortem
steps.body: The capstone isn't done until you've reflected. What did the agent do better than you expected? Where did it lose? What prompts would you reuse next time?
steps.verify: VerifyPOSTMORTEM.md exists, is 1-2 paragraphs, and lists at least one thing you'd do differently. You're done with the course.

quizzes.question: Q1. What is a *bad* capstone choice?

options.text: A bookmark organizer.
A clone of an existing major product.
A tip splitter for your friend group.
A tiny meeting-notes summarizer.
